title: Passwords and Hacking
objective: After this level you can explain common attacks on accounts and how to protect yours.
summary: Phishing, reused leaked passwords and guessing are common attacks. NIST and CISA advise long, unique passwords, a password manager and multifactor authentication.

cards.headline: "Password1!" follows the old rules perfectly. It's still a bad password.
cards.body: Sites that demand a capital, a number and a symbol push people toward exactly this kind of choice, notes NIST, the US standards agency, and attackers are likely to guess it. So how do accounts really get broken into, and what actually protects yours?

cards.headline: Three common ways in
cards.body: Phishing: a message with urgent language, a request for your details or a look-alike address such as amazan.com lures you to a fake page. A padlock doesn't prove a site is honest, the FBI warns; phishing sites use HTTPS too. Credential stuffing: username and password pairs leaked in one breach get tried on other sites. Guessing: attackers try common and previously leaked passwords first. None of these needs movie-style genius, just predictable habits.

cards.headline: Long beats clever
cards.body: NIST's 2025 guidance puts length first: at least 15 characters when a password is used on its own. Sites shouldn't force symbol mixes or scheduled changes, only a change after a breach. CISA suggests at least 16 characters, such as a passphrase of 4 to 7 unrelated words, and a different password for every account. A password manager makes that painless: it generates, stores and fills them in for you.

cards.fact: With multifactor authentication, a stolen password alone isn't enough.
cards.context: MFA asks for two or more ways to prove it's you, such as your password plus a code or a physical security key. CISA rates security keys as the best protection against phishing and text or email codes as the weakest. Even the weakest kind means a thief needs more than your password.

mascot.line: Long passphrase, one per account, a manager to remember them, MFA on top. That's the recipe.

cards.headline: Accounts: protected
learned: Phishing, credential stuffing and guessing are the common ways in
NIST (2025): length first, at least 15 characters for a password alone
Use a different password for every account, kept in a password manager
Turn on multifactor authentication; security keys resist phishing best

questions.prompt: NIST's 2025 password guidance puts one quality first. Which is it?

options.label: A mix of symbols, digits and capitals
options.rationale: NIST says sites shouldn't force those mixes.

options.label: Changing it on a regular schedule
options.rationale: Change it only after a breach.

options.label: A word you'll never forget, like a pet's name
options.rationale: Predictable words are among the first guesses.

questions.explanation: Under SP 800-63B-4, length comes first: at least 15 characters when the password is used alone.

questions.prompt: Why is reusing one password on many sites risky?

options.label: Websites share their passwords with each other
options.rationale: They don't need to: attackers try leaked pairs themselves.

options.label: A leak at one site lets attackers into the others
Reused passwords expire faster
options.rationale: Passwords don't wear out; change them after a breach.

options.label: It switches off multifactor authentication
options.rationale: MFA still helps; the reuse is the problem.

questions.explanation: In credential stuffing, pairs leaked in one breach are tried on other sites, so reuse spreads one leak to every account.

questions.prompt: Level 42's Morse code gave the commonest letter the shortest code. Which password attack also counts on what people use most often?

options.label: Phishing through a look-alike web address
options.rationale: Phishing tricks you with a fake page, not a common password.

options.label: Guessing common and leaked passwords first
Cracking the padlock's public-key encryption
options.rationale: The padlock only shows traffic is encrypted; attackers go around it.

options.label: Stealing a physical security key from a desk
options.rationale: Security keys are the best defense, not a common attack.

questions.explanation: Attackers try common and previously leaked passwords first, betting on predictable habits.
